Action de tondre la laine, la pelouse, etc.

examples.text: Faire la tonte.

La tonte des moutons s’effectue à peu près partout entre la fin du mois d’avril et le mois de mai ; en altitude les agneaux de moins d’un an seront tondus plus tard, en juillet-août, car ils sont encore sensibles au froid.

Coupe du gazon.

examples.text: Pour le compost « on jettera régulièrement toute une série de produits naturels : les détritus de jardin, les restes de la tonte du gazon, les épluchures de légumes...»
« Pour ne pas passer tout votre temps à désherber vos tomates, mulchez leurs pieds avec les chutes de tonte de la pelouse.»

glosses: Laine qu’on retire en tondant un troupeau.

examples.text: Ce troupeau appartenait au juge de Werst, le biró Koltz, lequel payait à la commune un gros droit de brébiage, et qui appréciait fort son pâtour Frik, le sachant très habile à la tonte, et très entendu au traitement des maladies, muguet, affilée, avertin, douve, encaussement, falère, clavelée, piétin, rabuze et autres affections d’origine pécuaire.

glosses: Temps où l’on tond les ovins.

examples.text: Pendant la tonte.

glosses: (Par métonymie) Par analogie avec la répétition des tontes de gazon, stratégie militaire où des attaques similaires sont régulièrement menées contre un ennemi pendant plusieurs années.

examples.text: Israël a été confronté au terrorisme dès le début de son histoire. Conscient de l’impossibilité de supprimer la menace, l’État hébreux a développé plusieurs techniques pour la réduire au maximum, la fameuse stratégie de « la tonte de gazon ».

glosses: To remove the fleece from (a sheep, llama, etc.) by clipping.

examples.text: shear the llamas

glosses: To cut the hair of (a person).

examples.text: shear the afro off someone's head

glosses: To cut, originally with a sword or other bladed weapon, now usually with shears, or as if using shears.

examples.text: So trenchant was the Templar’s weapon, that it shore asunder, as it had been a willow twig, the tough and plaited handle of the mace, which the ill-fated Saxon reared to parry the blow, and, descending on his head, levelled him with the earth.
the golden tresses […] were shorn away

glosses: To deform because of forces pushing in opposite directions.
To change in direction or speed.

examples.text: The total along-the-runway wind component sheared from an 8-knot headwind to about a 56-knot tailwind over a 44-second period.

glosses: To transform by displacing every point in a direction parallel to some given line by a distance proportional to the point’s distance from the line.
To make a vertical cut in coal.
(also 'shear off') To break or suddenly separate because of excessive force, eg. a bolt.
To reap, as grain.

examples.text:
Soon as the bending Scythe,
And Sickle keen, have shear'd the golden Grain,
Array'd in all the Equipage of Death,
Forth the stern Sportsman stalks

glosses: To deprive of property; to fleece.
A cutting tool similar to scissors, but often larger.

examples.text: short of their wool, and naked from the shear

glosses: A large machine use for cutting sheet metal.
The act of shearing, or something removed by shearing.

examples.text: After the second shearing, he is a two-shear ram; […] at the expiration of another year, he is a three-shear ram; the name always taking its date from the time of shearing.

glosses: Forces that push in opposite directions.
The phenomenon of wind shear.

examples.text: The first effect of a wind shear was detected at 34 to 42 seconds into the takeoff, at a speed of about 115 KIAS with the airplane about 3,800 feet down the runway. An average shear rate of about 2.5 knots per second resulted in an interruption in acceleration at this point with the airspeed remaining at 115 to 120 KIAS for 7 to 10 seconds.

glosses: A specific instance of wind shear.

examples.text: We hit a nasty shear on approach and had to go around.

glosses: A transformation that displaces every point in a direction parallel to some given line by a distance proportional to the point's distance from the line.
The response of a rock to deformation usually by compressive stress, resulting in particular textures.

glosses: To cut down grass or crops.

examples.text: He mowed the lawn every few weeks in the summer.

glosses: To cut down or slaughter in great numbers.

examples.text: In the afternoon they attacked again, in close formation: our artillery mowed them, but they came on and on, […]

On the one hand, we had a scenario where, effectively, the American admiral just went "You know what, all the destroyers attack", at which point they mowed through the Japanese destroyers like a Grim Reaper through a harvest of very, very dead gorn, especially with the Brooklyns in support.

glosses: The act of mowing (a garden, grass, etc.).

examples.text: The lawn hasn't had a mow for a couple of months, so it's like a jungle out there!

glosses: A shot played with a sweeping or scythe-like motion.

examples.text: I consider it would engender a stiff, tame, cautious mode of play, with only now and then a mow, or a chopping hit.
At times, they seemed to be playing an especially orgiastic version of Stick Cricket, all computerised mows over midwicket and 30 off the over.

glosses: A scornful grimace; a wry face.

examples.text: Those that paint them dying […] delineate the prisoners spitting in their executioners faces, and making mowes at them.
Make mows at him.

glosses: To make grimaces, mock.

examples.text: For every trifle are they set upon me: / Sometime like apes that mow and chatter at me, / And after bite me;
Nodding, becking, and mowing.
He mowed at me, and, bowing with ironical politeness, pointed to the house.
